title: Alignment and object layout
objectives: Work out a struct's size and padding, and reorder its fields to shrink it.

screens.title: Where is the padding
screens.prose: `struct S { uint8_t a; double b; uint8_t c; };` takes 24 bytes. Pointers are 4 bytes in this app and 8 on a desktop, so every struct here uses fixed-width fields.

state.caption: 24 bytes, numbered by offset. Each row is 8 bytes.

screens.question: Tap every byte that is padding.

hints.text: A `double` likes to start at a multiple of 8.
So `b` sits at bytes 8 to 15.
Bytes 1 to 7 and 17 to 23 hold nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where `b` must start, then where the struct must end.

byKey.r2c1: Byte 8 is where `b` starts, so it is not padding.
byKey.r1c2: Bytes 1 to 7 are skipped so `b` can start at 8.
byKey.r3c2: Bytes 17 to 23 are padding too: the size rounds up to 24.

explain.text: `b` must start at a multiple of 8, so bytes 1 to 7 are skipped. The size rounds up to a multiple of 8, so bytes 17 to 23 are skipped. 14 of the 24 bytes hold nothing.

screens.title: Shuffle the fields
screens.prose: The same three fields, `a` (1 byte), `b` (8 bytes) and `c` (1 byte), in three orders. Slide through them and read each size.

state.caption: Order a, b, c: 24 bytes, 14 of them padding (·).

frames.caption: Order a, b, c: 24 bytes, 14 of them padding (·).
Order a, c, b: 16 bytes, 6 of them padding (·).
Order b, a, c: 16 bytes, 6 of them padding (·).

screens.question: What is the smallest size you can reach?

hints.text: Watch where the 8-byte field lands in each order.
Order b, a, c packs `a` and `c` side by side.
Two orders reach 16 bytes.

feedback.correct: 16 bytes, from 24, just by moving a field.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to order b, a, c and read the caption.

byKey.sum: 10 is the sum of the fields. The struct still rounds up to a multiple of 8.
byKey.same: 24 is the declared order. Try the other two.

explain.text: Keeping the 1-byte fields together leaves one gap of 6 bytes instead of two gaps of 7. Field order changes the size; the fields do not.

canvas.caption: Order b, a, c: 16 bytes, 6 of them padding (·).

screens.title: Offsets
screens.prose: Each field starts at the next multiple of its **alignment**, which for these fixed-width scalars equals its size. The bytes skipped are **padding**. The size rounds up to the largest alignment, so an array of structs stays aligned.

state.caption: 24 bytes, numbered by offset. Each row is 8 bytes.

screens.question: Fill in the offsets and the size of `S`.

hints.text: Where is the first multiple of 8 after byte 0?
`b` ends at byte 16, so `c` sits there.
Offsets 0, 8 and 16; size 24.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place each field at the next multiple of its size.

byKey.r1c1: A `double` aligns to 8: the first multiple of 8 after byte 1 is 8.
byKey.r3c2: 17 bytes round up to a multiple of 8, the largest alignment: 24.

explain.text: `a` at 0, `b` at 8, `c` at 16, and 17 rounds up to 24. The tail padding lets `S[1].b` start on a multiple of 8 too. Moved first, `b` gives offsets 0, 8, 9 and size 16.

screens.title: An order message
screens.prose: A message from an exchange, decoded into a struct. Every field is 1, 2 or 4 bytes, so the alignment is at most 4.
screens.question: Fill in the offsets and the size, as declared.

hints.text: `type` ends at 1, and `seq` needs a multiple of 4.
Each 1-byte or 2-byte field before a 4-byte one leaves a gap.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each 4-byte field needs an offset that is a multiple of 4.

byKey.r1c1: `type` ends at byte 1, and the next multiple of 4 is 4.
byKey.r8c1: `time` ends at 32, already a multiple of 4.

explain.text: Three small fields each sit before a 4-byte field, so each leaves a gap: 3, 3 and 2 bytes. The 24 bytes of data take 32.

screens.title: Largest first
screens.prose: Sort the fields from largest to smallest. The 4-byte fields go first, then `instrument`, then the two single bytes.
screens.question: Fill in the sorted size and the memory for a million orders.

hints.text: Five 4-byte fields fill 0 to 19.
`instrument` at 20, `type` at 22, `side` at 23.
24 bytes; 32 MB against 24 MB.

feedback.correct: 24 bytes: 25% smaller, 24 MB instead of 32 MB.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place the sorted fields one after another.

byKey.r1c1: Offsets 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 22 and 23 end at 24, a multiple of 4.
byKey.r0c2: 32 bytes times a million is 32 MB.
byKey.r1c2: 24 bytes times a million is 24 MB.

explain.text: Sorted, the offsets are 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 22 and 23: 24 bytes, no padding. A million orders take 24 MB, not 32 MB: a quarter fewer cache lines to fill.

screens.title: Write the size rule
screens.prose: Each field is aligned to its own size of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. The fields arrive as a list of sizes in declaration order.
screens.question: Fix `struct_size` and `best_size`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Fifteen hidden tests on both functions. They include this lesson's structs, an empty struct, one field and a struct sorting cannot shrink.

hints.text: The starter sums the sizes and never pads.
Round the offset up to a multiple of `s` before each field. Round the end up to the widest field.
`offset = (offset + s - 1) / s * s;` then `offset += s;`, and sort a copy with `std::greater<int>()`.

feedback.correct: That's it. Round up before each field, and once at the end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: `(offset + s - 1) / s * s` rounds up to a multiple of `s`. The last rounding uses the widest field, which is the struct's alignment. An empty struct is 0 in this model, though C++ makes it 1.

screens.title: A quick-fire size
screens.prose: The interviewer asks it quick-fire: `struct T { char a; double b; char c; };`.
screens.question: What is `sizeof(T)`?

options.why: You summed the fields; padding is part of the size.
You placed `c` at 16 but forgot the tail padding to a multiple of 8.
16 is the size with `c` moved next to `a`. Here the order is as declared.

hints.text: Where does `b` start?
`b` starts at 8, and `c` at 16.
17 rounds up to a multiple of 8: 24.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place each field, then round the end up.

byKey.b: Adding 1 + 8 + 1 is the blurt. The `double` needs offset 8, and the end rounds to 24.
byKey.c: 17 is where the data ends. The size rounds up so the next `T` in an array starts aligned.

explain.text: `a` at 0, `b` at 8, `c` at 16, then round 17 up to 24. Summing the fields gives 10, which is never right here. Padding is part of the size.

screens.title: When sorting saves nothing
screens.prose: Sorting is not magic. This struct already pairs each small field with the next.

params.title: Fields of 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes, twice
lines: struct A { uint8_t a; uint16_t b; uint32_t c; double d;
uint8_t e; uint16_t f; uint32_t g; double h; };

screens.question: Fill in both sizes.

hints.text: The first half fills exactly 16 bytes with one byte of padding.
32 both ways.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Lay out the first four fields and see where `d` ends.

byKey.r0c1: `a` 0, `b` 2, `c` 4, `d` 8 to 15, and the second half repeats from 16.
byKey.r1c1: Sorted: two doubles, two `uint32_t`, two `uint16_t`, two bytes: 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 30, rounded to 32.

explain.text: As declared, each half packs into 16 bytes with one padding byte. Sorted, 30 bytes of data round up to 32. And `struct { uint16_t; uint8_t; }` is 4, not 3: tail padding cannot be sorted away.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
Every layout today followed two rules. With $e$ the end of the previous field and $a$ a field's alignment:

$$\text{offset} = a \left\lceil \frac{e}{a} \right\rceil, \qquad \text{size} = a_{\max} \left\lceil \frac{e_{\text{last}}}{a_{\max}} \right\rceil$$

Sorting largest first wastes least.
screens.question: What is `sizeof` of `struct { uint32_t a; uint16_t b; double c; }`?

options.why: You summed the fields; `c` still needs an offset that is a multiple of 8.
You padded `b` to 8 bytes. `b` needs a multiple of 2, so `c` fits at 8.

hints.text: Place `a` and `b` first.
They end at 6, so `c` starts at 8.
`c` ends at 16, a multiple of 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the two rules field by field.

explain.text: `a` at 0, `b` at 4, `c` at 8, ending at 16. Sixteen is a multiple of 8, so there is no tail padding.

screens.title: Drill: sizes
screens.prose: Drill: about 90 seconds a struct. Say the offsets aloud first. Byte counts are exact; only costs in this course are round figures. Sizes are in bytes, in declaration order.
screens.question: Fill in each size, as declared and sorted largest first.

hints.text: Lay each one out byte by byte.
16 and 12; 48 and 32; 4 and 4; 16 and 16.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: End 13 rounds up to a multiple of 4: 16.
byKey.r1c1: Each 1-byte field before a double costs 7 bytes of padding.
byKey.r1c2: Three doubles, then three bytes: 27, rounded to 32.
byKey.r2c1: 3 bytes round up to a multiple of 2: 4.
byKey.r3c1: 12 bytes round up to a multiple of 8: 16.

explain.text: Every answer is place, pad, round. Sorting helps when small fields sit between big ones. It cannot remove tail padding.

screens.title: Follow-up: on the wire and in a line
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: can I `memcpy` the 24-byte order onto the wire? No: padding and byte order differ by platform, so the bytes are written by hand. There is a second cost here too.

state.caption: Each cell is 8 bytes; each number is one 24-byte struct.

screens.question: Each row is one 64-byte line. Of the first 8 structs, how many cross a line boundary?

hints.text: Find the structs whose cells sit in two rows.
Struct 2 starts at byte 48 and ends at byte 71.
Structs 2 and 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a number that appears in two rows.

byKey.none: 64 is not a multiple of 24, so some structs must cross.
byKey.three: Struct 7 ends at byte 191, inside line 2.
byKey.all: Most structs sit inside one line.

explain.text: Structs 2 and 5 each touch two lines, so reading one can cost two misses. Padded to 32 bytes, two fit in each line and none cross. And a `uint16_t` flag appended to the 24-byte struct makes it 28 bytes, not 26.

ideas: Each field starts at the next multiple of its alignment; the skipped bytes are padding.
A struct's size rounds up to its largest alignment, so arrays of it stay aligned.
Sorting fields largest first wastes least, but cannot remove tail padding.

formula.name: Offset of a field
formula.note: e: where the previous field ends; a: this field's alignment.

summary.trap: Summing the field sizes: `{char, double, char}` is 24 bytes, not 10.

quiz.prose: A colleague sends an order to another machine with `memcpy` of the whole struct.
quiz.question: Is that safe?

options.text: No: padding and byte order can differ
Yes: a struct is just its bytes
options.why: Its bytes include padding, and the other side may lay them out differently.

options.text: Yes, if both machines use the same compiler
options.why: A packing flag or a different compiler version can still change the padding, and byte order belongs to the CPU, not the compiler.

options.text: Only if the struct is under 64 bytes
options.why: Size is not the problem. Layout is.

feedback.correct: No. A wire format fixes every byte itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What must both ends agree on?

explain.text: Padding bytes are garbage and the byte order is the platform's. A wire format states each field's offset and byte order. Level 3 builds one.

quiz.prose: `struct { uint8_t a; uint32_t b; uint16_t c; }`
quiz.question: What is its size in bytes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place each field, then round the end up to 4.

byKey.sum: 7 is the sum of the fields.
byKey.tail: 10 is where `c` ends. Round up to a multiple of 4.

explain.text: `a` at 0, `b` at 4, `c` at 8, ending at 10. The largest alignment is 4, so the size is 12.

quiz.question: What is the size, sorted largest first?

byKey.sum: 7 is where the data ends. Round up to 4.

explain.text: `b` at 0, `c` at 4, `a` at 6, ending at 7, rounded up to 8. Sorting saved a third.

quiz.prose: The sorted 24-byte order struct (largest field 4 bytes) gains a `uint16_t` flag at the end.
quiz.question: What is its new size?

widget.accept: 28: 26 rounded up to a multiple of 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does the flag end, and what is the largest alignment?

byKey.sum: 26 is where the flag ends. Round up to a multiple of 4.
byKey.eight: No field is 8 bytes, so round to 4, not 8.

explain.text: The flag sits at 24 and ends at 26. The struct's alignment is 4, so it rounds up to 28.
